overview: Healthpeak Properties is a Denver-headquartered, S&P 500 healthcare REIT that owns, operates, and develops real estate focused on healthcare discovery and delivery across the United States. The company is organized into three core segments -- outpatient medical, lab (life science), and senior housing -- and significantly expanded its outpatient medical footprint via its March 2024 merger of equals with Physicians Realty Trust. In March 2026, Healthpeak spun off its senior housing/life plan community portfolio into a separately traded REIT, Janus Living, Inc. (NYSE: JAN), which it continues to consolidate and externally manage while retaining roughly 69% economic and voting interest as of Q3 2026.

business_model.summary: Healthpeak earns rental income from long-term, often triple-net leases on outpatient medical buildings and lab/life-science buildings leased to healthcare providers, hospital systems, and biotech/pharma tenants, plus resident fee income from senior housing communities (now housed in consolidated subsidiary Janus Living) operated under RIDEA structures with third-party operators. As a REIT, it must distribute at least 90% of taxable income, so growth is funded largely through capital markets access, joint ventures, and asset recycling rather than retained earnings.

revenue_streams.name: Senior Housing (resident fees, via Janus Living)
Other non-reportable (loans receivable, preferred equity, other)

business_model.customer_type: B2B -- hospital systems, physician groups, biotech/pharma/medical device companies, and senior housing operators; RIDEA structure for senior housing creates indirect B2C exposure to residents
business_model.geographic_mix: All U.S.; outpatient medical diversified nationally (large hospital-system relationships incl. HCA ~7% of total revenue); lab concentrated in South San Francisco (59% of lab sq ft), Boston (22%), and San Diego (17%); senior housing concentrated in Florida and Texas

competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest diversified healthcare REITs by enterprise value, with scale leadership in outpatient medical (post-Physicians Realty merger) and a top-tier concentrated lab portfolio in the three leading U.S. life-science hubs; smaller and more leveraged to life science than Welltower/Ventas, which skew more toward senior housing/CCRC operating leverage.

moat_factors.description: 79% of outpatient medical buildings are on or adjacent to hospital campuses and 96% are affiliated with hospital systems, creating sticky tenant relationships and high switching costs for physician tenants
Properties concentrated in established, supply-constrained life-science submarkets (South SF, Boston, San Diego) with specialized, costly-to-replicate infrastructure (fume hoods, floor loads, HVAC)

moat_factors.factor: Investment-grade balance sheet / cost of capital
moat_factors.description: Investment-grade ratings and staggered, largely fixed-rate debt support lower funding costs than smaller healthcare landlords, aiding acquisition competitiveness

moat_factors.factor: Diversification across three healthcare real estate verticals
moat_factors.description: Outpatient medical, lab, and (via Janus Living) senior housing provide some counter-cyclical balance versus single-segment peers

weaknesses: Highly specialized, costly tenant improvements for lab and outpatient medical space raise re-leasing costs and lengthen downtime versus generic office/industrial REITs
Lab segment occupancy and NOI have deteriorated sharply amid biotech funding softness and new supply, exposing concentration risk in just three submarkets

RIDEA-structured senior housing (now largely housed in Janus Living) exposes Healthpeak's TRS to full operating risk, including labor costs, litigation, and regulatory compliance, rather than a pure landlord position
Complex post-spinoff relationship with Janus Living creates governance/conflict-of-interest questions and economic exposure to a separately traded stock
No. 1-2 tenants (HCA ~15% of outpatient medical segment revenue) create meaningful single-tenant concentration risk

growth_drivers: Lab leasing recovery: Q3 2026 lab leasing of 480,000 sq ft (strongest in over a year) plus 643,000 sq ft executed/under LOI post quarter-end, with total portfolio lab occupancy up 270 bps since year-end 2025
Outpatient medical internal growth via mark-to-market lease renewals, annual rent escalations, and percentage rent increases, aided by property-management internalization cost savings

Janus Living platform: externally managed senior housing REIT generating management fees and capital-recycling optionality, with $2.26 billion of senior housing acquisitions completed in the first nine months of 2026 (SWF JV buyout, Sterling Estates, etc.)

Capital recycling / joint ventures: formation of the Brookfield JV (49% stake sale of 86 outpatient medical buildings at a ~$2.1 billion valuation) and other partial dispositions to fund new investment while retaining management control and upside call rights
Demographic tailwinds: aging U.S. population supports long-term demand for outpatient medical and senior housing real estate
Continued de-risking/simplification of the balance sheet through asset sales, debt repayment, and diversified financing (term loans, unsecured notes, commercial paper)

business.description: Total portfolio lab occupancy fell to 85.9% at Q3 2026 from 93.4% a year earlier (same-store occupancy 90.6%); same-store lab NOI declined 0.7% in Q3 and 3.9% for the first nine months of 2026 amid reduced biotech funding, industry consolidation, and new supply in South SF, Boston, and San Diego; FY2025 included a $176 million impairment tied to South SF/Needham lab joint ventures

HCA Healthcare represents ~15% of outpatient medical segment revenue (~7% of total); CommonSpirit Health ~6%/3%; financial distress at a major hospital system or operator could materially affect occupancy and collections

Senior housing (via Janus Living) depends on third-party operators for day-to-day management; the TRS bears nearly all operational, regulatory, and litigation risk despite limited control over operators
Lease rejection in bankruptcy caps unsecured claims and can force costly transitions to replacement tenants or operators, magnified where multiple properties are under a single master lease

financial.description: Outstanding indebtedness of approximately $9.8 billion at year-end 2025; sizable 2027 term loan and senior notes maturities create refinancing risk if rates stay elevated or credit spreads widen

Variable-rate borrowings (revolver, commercial paper, term loans) and upcoming refinancings are sensitive to SOFR; a Fed funds rate increase in September 2026 and persistent inflation have raised borrowing costs

financial.risk: Economic exposure to Janus Living's stock price
financial.description: Healthpeak retains ~69% economic/voting interest in a separately traded, smaller-cap REIT (Janus Living); Janus Living stock volatility and Healthpeak's limited ability to easily dispose of the stake create valuation and liquidity risk

Mortgage, term loan, and unsecured note covenants (leverage ratios, tangible net worth, coverage ratios) constrain operational flexibility; Janus Living's credit facility carries its own covenant package

regulatory.description: Reduced Medicaid spending, expiring ACA subsidies, and provisions of the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' disproportionately affect non-expansion states and could pressure tenant/operator reimbursement and liquidity
Tenants and RIDEA operators face Stark Law, anti-kickback, false claims act, and state licensure/CON exposure; violations can trigger sanctions that impair their ability to pay rent
Proposed legislation restricting REIT ownership of healthcare real estate, or changes to RIDEA/TRS tax treatment, could directly affect structure and economics

regulatory.risk: NIH funding and life-science policy uncertainty
regulatory.description: Federal workforce reductions, NIH grant funding cuts/indirect cost caps, and visa policy changes affecting the scientific workforce have reduced life-science tenant demand and investor funding, directly pressuring the lab segment

macro.description: Lab tenants' ability to lease space depends on venture capital and public-market funding availability; a prolonged biotech funding downturn would continue to pressure lab occupancy and rents

macro.risk: Elevated interest rates / cap rate pressure
macro.description: Higher rates increase borrowing costs, pressure asset valuations, and compress deal flow/competition for acquisitions
Senior housing and healthcare facility operators face rising wage and staffing costs that can erode margins if not passed through via rates
Tariff actions have raised construction and tenant-improvement costs, pressuring development/redevelopment yields

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Diversified healthcare real estate benefits from secular aging-population demand; outpatient medical is viewed as defensive/resilient, senior housing is in a cyclical upswing (strong 2026 occupancy and rate growth), while the life-science/lab subsector remains in an oversupply-driven downturn with signs of stabilizing leasing activity in late 2026
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate -- outpatient medical and triple-net leases provide stable, recurring cash flow; lab and RIDEA senior housing are more cyclical, tied to biotech funding cycles and consumer/senior spending respectively
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high -- REIT cost of capital, acquisition yields, variable-rate debt costs, and asset valuations are directly sensitive to rate moves
key_input_costs: Construction materials and labor (tenant improvements, redevelopment)

recent_developments.event: Completed Janus Living IPO: 48.3 million Class A-1 shares sold at $20.00, generating $966 million gross proceeds; Healthpeak retained 138.8 million shares plus OP units, becoming Janus Living's majority owner and external manager
Janus Living June follow-on offering of 28.75 million shares (incl. full over-allotment) generated $719 million gross proceeds
Janus Living August follow-on offering of 18.4 million shares generated $534 million gross proceeds; Healthpeak's economic/voting interest in Janus Living settled at ~69.2% as of Q3 2026

Formed a joint venture with an affiliate of Brookfield Asset Management, contributing 86 outpatient medical buildings across 11 states; Brookfield acquired a 49% stake at a ~$2.1 billion gross valuation, with Healthpeak retaining management control and a post-year-7 call right
Paid $105 million to acquire the senior construction loan on a two-building San Diego lab campus and subsequently obtained 100% ownership (the 'HQ Point Buyout')

Reported Q3 2026 results: raised full-year FFO as Adjusted guidance to $1.76-$1.78 per share and raised same-store cash NOI growth guidance to 0.5%-2.0%; lab leasing of 480,000 sq ft was the strongest quarter in over a year, though lab same-store NOI still declined 0.7%; GAAP diluted EPS guidance was lowered to $0.39-$0.41 due to Janus Living senior-housing depreciation, with no impact on FFO as Adjusted
Acquired the remaining 46.5% interest in the SWF SH JV (19 senior housing assets) for $312 million, taking the portfolio to 100% ownership ahead of contribution to Janus Living

Recorded a $176 million impairment related to South San Francisco and Needham, MA lab joint ventures amid life-science oversupply and weaker biotech capital raising; total lab portfolio occupancy fell from 97.5% to 88.2% during 2025

items.notes: Up $0.02 at the midpoint from prior guidance of $1.73-$1.77; third guidance raise of 2026
Reduction driven by incremental depreciation/amortization from Janus Living senior housing acquisitions; excluded from Nareit FFO/FFO as Adjusted, so no impact on those metrics
Raised 50 bps at midpoint; segment detail: outpatient medical 2.5%-3.0%, lab (3.0%)-(6.0)%, senior housing 16%-19%
Reflects continued occupancy pressure despite improving leasing volumes; management expects lease-up to take 2-3 years

items.metric: Senior housing same-store cash NOI growth
items.notes: Driven by rate growth, occupancy gains, and the SWF JV buyout; reported through consolidated Janus Living

guidance.management_commentary: Management characterized Q3 2026 lab leasing (480,000 sq ft, plus 643,000 sq ft executed or under LOI since quarter-end) as the strongest in over a year and a sign of inflecting demand, while cautioning that reported occupancy may optically decline further as new leases commence and that stabilization/lease-up of vacant lab space is expected to take two to three years. Outpatient medical and senior housing were described as performing in line with or ahead of expectations, supporting the overall guidance raise even as GAAP EPS guidance was cut for non-cash depreciation reasons tied to the Janus Living portfolio.

bull_case: Lab leasing has clearly inflected higher (strongest quarterly volume in over a year plus a large forward pipeline), suggesting the worst of the life-science downturn may be behind the portfolio, with upside optionality if biotech funding recovers
Outpatient medical segment delivers steady, defensive same-store NOI growth (~3%) with high hospital-system affiliation, providing a stable cash-flow base

Janus Living spinoff unlocked capital (nearly $2.2 billion of gross IPO/follow-on proceeds) while preserving management fee income and majority economic exposure to a fast-growing senior housing platform (16-19% same-store NOI growth guided)
Active capital recycling (Brookfield JV, asset sales) funds growth and reduces leverage without diluting common equity as heavily as a straight equity raise
Management has raised full-year FFO as Adjusted guidance three times during 2026, signaling positive momentum into 2027
bear_case: Lab segment occupancy (85.9% total portfolio, down from 93.4% a year ago) and same-store NOI (down 3.9% YTD) remain in decline, and guidance still implies a further 3-6% same-store NOI contraction for the segment in FY2026

Structural oversupply in core lab submarkets (South SF, Boston, San Diego) combined with reduced NIH funding, visa/workforce policy uncertainty, and tighter biotech VC funding could prolong the downturn beyond management's 2-3 year lease-up timeline

Complexity and conflicts of interest introduced by the Janus Living external-management relationship (economic exposure to a separately traded, smaller REIT, potential governance conflicts) add a layer of risk not present in a simpler REIT structure
Roughly $9.8 billion of debt and ongoing refinancing needs (e.g., 2027 term loan maturities) leave the company exposed if interest rates stay elevated or credit conditions tighten

GAAP EPS guidance cut and historical lab impairments ($176 million in FY2025) underscore that reported earnings quality and asset values in the life-science book remain under pressure despite the FFO narrative
